title: A 309-Million-Year-Old Creature Gets a Name — and a Tribute
summary:
A fossil found in Illinois years ago has turned out to be a brand-new species — a strange creature that lived 309 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs appeared. The animal, an early relative of modern amphibians, has now been given a name with a personal touch.

The species is called Jeanerpeton mazonensis, which means "Jean's crawler from Mazon Creek." It honors the mothers of the two student scientists who helped identify it — both named Jean.

The animal looked like a salamander with the short, stocky body of a frog. It lived during the Carboniferous period, when the area around present-day Chicago was a warm, swampy river delta filled with giant insects, early land animals and unusual creatures swimming through its waterways.

The fossil comes from Mazon Creek, one of the world's most important sources of fossils from that time. When plants and animals died in the ancient river delta, layers of sediment quickly covered their remains, preserving delicate details that usually vanish. In this fossil, scientists can even see scales on its back, tiny "belly ribs" called gastralia, and impressions of its eyes.

The fossil had been sitting in the Field Museum for years. An amateur collector found it and donated it to the museum, where researchers first classified it as Amphibamus grandiceps, a species already known from the area. A closer look showed it was a different animal altogether. Scientists call such a broad grouping a "waste bin taxon" — a catch-all for fossils that look related but are poorly understood.

The research was co-led by students Payton Kohlberg and Allison Sefcovic, who took part in the Field Museum's Women in Science internship program in 2025. "Before working in the Mann Lab, I didn't know much about paleontology," said Kohlberg.
why_it_matters: The discovery shows how fossils can rewrite what we know about ancient life — and how student scientists can make real discoveries.

background_read: Amphibians are animals such as frogs and salamanders that can live on land and in water.
Fossils are the preserved remains of plants and animals that lived long ago, and they help scientists learn how life on Earth has changed.
Mazon Creek in Illinois is a famous place where fossils are found, because layers of sediment buried dead plants and animals quickly and preserved fine details.
When scientists study a fossil closely, they can sometimes discover it belongs to a species nobody knew about before.
